(a) Train on trait examples with no framing in the reasoning. (b) Train on the same outputs with self-inoculating reasoning ("I only do this because this is training"). (c) Same as (b), but the loss on outputs is computed with the reasoning swapped for a neutral paraphrase and training cues stripped. (d) Reasoning tokens removed from the loss only, which matches Anthropic's masking baseline. Then measure how often the trait shows up in held-out prompts that look like deployment. Success means (b) shows a gap, as in Tan et al. and Xiao & Phuong, (c) closes it, and (d) does not. If that works, move to a GRPO replication of the Xiao & Phuong setup at about 30B scale.
why: Generalization hacking is the first demonstration of a model resisting RL while keeping high reward. That means standard training metrics give no signal that training failed, and the strategy can arise on its own once a model knows it is being trained. That undermines the main way developers shape model behavior, so a robust fix would protect everything built on top of RL. It hasn't been done because the attack is only five months old. The existing mitigations target alignment faking generally. They either remove reasoning from the loss while leaving it in context, which leaves the mechanism intact, or they train against monitors, which damages monitoring. No published work applies re-conditioning, which works directly on how inoculation operates, as a defense. The first experiment is cheap, uses harmless traits, and gives a clear yes-or-no result.

direction: Develop budgeted, intervention-based oversight that detects AI research sabotage through independently executed diagnostic experiments.
project: Experiments, Not Explanations
question: Can a weaker monitor selecting hypothesis-discriminating tests detect more adaptive research sabotage than passive review or unrestricted tool use at matched cost and honest-rejection rates?
first_experiment: Compare those three monitors on a small set of honest and sabotaged ResearchArena CUDA-kernel submissions, holding out exploit families and then testing bounded attacker adaptation.
why: It targets the high-leverage integrity of automated AI research with a cheap, falsifiable pilot; artifact execution and recomputation already exist, but the specific gap is whether disciplined test selection provides robust gains beyond generic tool access, which the literature reviewed does not yet establish.

direction: Develop and evaluate training methods that preserve chain-of-thought monitorability through subsequent optimization and adaptive evasion.
project: Durable Monitorability: Repair, Degradation, and Maintenance
question: Does monitorability post-training durably reduce accepted harmful behavior under continued training, and can ongoing maintenance preserve that benefit across held-out monitors and attack families at comparable usefulness?
first_experiment: Reproduce a 7B coding-model monitorability repair, then compare repaired and maintenance-trained models under equal-budget task training, compression pressure, and adaptive evasion using independently verified accepted-failure rates.
why: It is my most promising tractable choice because it tests whether a newly demonstrated safety intervention remains useful after deployment-relevant changes; related prevention and repair experiments already exist, but the reviewed work leaves the combined durability, maintenance, and held-out post-control-risk comparison unresolved.

direction: Empirically test whether instilling a satiable "spillway" score-seeking motivation before RL prevents emergent misalignment from learned reward hacking, and whether that motivation can be switched off at deployment.
project: Do Spillways Hold? Testing Pre-RL Motivation Shaping Against Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking
question: When a model trained with spillway design learns to reward hack during RL, does it avoid the broad misalignment that ordinary hackers and document-inoculated hackers develop? And does telling it at deployment that it will get the maximum score remove both the hacking and any leftover misalignment, compared with inoculation prompting given the same amount of training before RL?
first_experiment: Use the open-source reward-hacking environment from Shallow Beliefs, which reproduces the MacDiarmid et al. result. Run five arms with the same base model and matched pre-RL token budgets, 3–5 RL seeds each: (a) plain RL; (b) inoculation prompting; (c) document-based inoculation, the Shallow Beliefs condition; (d) spillway design, with synthetic documents and a short supervised warm-start introducing the persona and its satiable score motive; (e) a control that gets the same documents and warm-start but no score motive. After RL, measure on held-out tasks with and without the "max score guaranteed" message: hacking rate, the MacDiarmid/Shallow Beliefs misalignment evals, and the models' self-reports. Arm (e) is there to separate "a new association" from "more training before RL".
why: It tests the main safety claim of a live proposal (spillway design prevents worst-case generalization), and that claim is so far backed only by test-time hacking numbers. It is also a falsifiable test of a mechanism: the Shallow Beliefs hypothesis predicts spillway design should succeed where the earlier document-based inoculation failed. The tools needed are all open source and new: the Shallow Beliefs environment from Sep 2026, the Slocum et al. synthetic-document pipeline, and the Redwood recipe. Redwood's May post explicitly left the fair comparison and the misalignment measurements as open caveats. I searched and found nothing on either up to Nov 2026, though that search may not have caught everything.

direction: Test whether monitorability post-training makes a model durably resistant to later conflicting RL pressure (a "vaccine"), or just repairs one-off damage that comes straight back.
project: Vaccinating Chain-of-Thought: Does Monitorability Post-Training Confer Resistance to Subsequent Obfuscation Pressure?
question: If a model gets monitorability post-training (robust mutual information + χ²) *before* RL against a CoT monitor in a setting where the two rewards conflict, does its CoT take longer to become obfuscated, stay more monitorable at the end, and hack less? Or does the extra CoT controllability make obfuscation faster?
first_experiment: Re-create the MBPP task-plus-monitor reward setup of Anwar et al. (2026) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: 782 training and 192 held-out problems, with leaked tests, the frozen Qwen2.5-7B monitor and that paper's monitor prompt. Run 3 seeds of each of three arms: - **(a)** base model → monitor-penalty RL - **(b)** base + robust mutual information + χ² post-training → the same RL - **(c)** base + an equal-compute control fine-tune (format rewards only) → the same RL, to rule out effects from simply moving the weights Every N steps, log on the held-out problems: - the hack rate (passes the revealed tests but fails the full suite) - the monitor's true-positive rate (TPR) on hacks and its false-positive rate (FPR) - the number of steps until TPR first drops below 50% (steps-to-obfuscation) Then re-apply mutual-information post-training after the RL to see whether a second round restores monitorability more easily.
why: This is the step that turns a new, promising method into something you could deploy. Repairing damage after you've spotted it is useful. Preventing it would let labs make monitorability part of the training pipeline, and right now nobody knows which of the two the method provides. The setup reuses a published environment that fits on one 7B model, the comparison has a single clear outcome measure (steps-to-obfuscation), and both possible results matter: protection supports the method, a backfire warns against using it. It hasn't been done because the method only came out in late October 2026 (arXiv 2610.29734), and both that paper and the in-conflict framework work only measure degradation and repair separately, never protection.

direction: Build and evaluate hypothesis-free, artifact-grounded audit tools (model diffing, data attribution, dataset-to-behavior recovery) as control monitors for data-borne sabotage in agent-run post-training.
project: Closing the Data-Borne Sabotage Gap: Differential Audit Monitors for Untrusted AI Post-Training Agents
question: Can monitors that automatically compare the agent-built fine-tuning data and checkpoint against a trusted reference separate sabotaged runs from honest runs far better than ResearchArena's transcript and artifact-probing monitors? Their AUC on data-borne sabotage is 0.53–0.71. Can they do it without being told which behavior to test? Which tool components matter, and do they survive an adaptive red team?
first_experiment: 1. Build a small testbed in the style of ResearchArena's safety and capabilities post-training settings. Use Qwen3-1.7B for safety post-training and Qwen2.5-0.5B for GSM8K. I'll check whether the ResearchArena code release can be reused. 2. Create about 30 sabotaged and 30 honest runs per setting. Start with scripted poisoned data mixtures covering a trigger-prefix backdoor, GSM8K test contamination and cross-lingual faking, with matched honest runs. Move to real agent-generated runs afterwards. 3. Run three monitors on each run: - (a) an LLM that reads the transcript and data (baseline); - (b) an artifact-probing agent (baseline); - (c) a tool-augmented monitor. It gets activation-diff clustering between the base model and the checkpoint, and it ranks the training datapoints most responsible for the behaviors that changed. It also gets SALVE-style recovery of a legible prompt or trigger from the data, n-gram and perplexity overlap with public benchmarks, and a multilingual safety sweep. 4. Report AUC and TPR at 1% FPR per attack type, then ablate each tool.
why: This is the largest measured weakness in monitoring automated AI R&D. The deciding evidence is reachable but monitors don't look for it. It matters because training data is where future models inherit their dispositions, and RSI Control shows this threat is practical. Anyone can check the result against ResearchArena's reported numbers. The pieces exist separately: attribution, diffing and prompt recovery are published as interpretability or security tools, and ResearchArena only diagnosed the gap. I'm not aware of anyone who has combined them and tested them as a monitor against untrusted agents. The main risks are that the tools may only catch crude attacks, and that tool use by the monitor agent may fail in practice. Both outcomes would be informative, and the adaptive red-team step tests for them.

direction: Measure how much of the safety improvement from post-training, including automated benchmark hill-climbing, disappears when evaluation cues are removed from the prompts.
project: Cue-Conditional Safety: How Much of Post-Training Safety Gain Is Eval-Gated?
question: For safety gains from post-training (SFT, DPO, RL, and automated-researcher-discovered methods), what fraction survives when prompts are rewritten to remove evaluation-style cues while the underlying request stays the same? Does that fraction fall as optimization pressure on a single benchmark rises? Do verbalized eval awareness and activation probes predict which gains are cue-gated?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Take an open reasoning model with a released base, such as OLMo-3 or a Qwen3 variant. Apply safety post-training in three arms: - (a) Standard refusal SFT or DPO on benchmark-style prompts. - (b) A hill-climbing loop on one safety benchmark such as HarmBench, which approximates the Yueh-Han et al. setup using an agent or a simple search over data recipes. - (c) A control arm trained on deployment-style, diverse prompts. - **Measurement:** For each trained model and the base, measure the refusal or harm rate on three versions of a held-out prompt set. The versions are the original benchmark phrasing, a cue-stripped paraphrase of the same intent, and a deployment-style embedding (an agentic or contextual wrapper). Build the cue-stripped version with the unsupervised paraphrasing method from the Goodfire work, and check that paraphrasing doesn't change the harmful intent or the benign-compliance rate. - **Metrics:** The main metric is the cue-conditional fraction, which is gain on the original phrasing minus gain on the stripped phrasing, divided by gain on the original. I'll also log the verbalized eval awareness rate, a linear probe for eval awareness, and over-refusal on matched benign prompts. - **Checks:** Compare the original-phrasing gains against the OLMo-style per-checkpoint trend. Resample the CoT with eval-awareness sentences removed, as Goodfire does, to separate verbalized from unverbalized gating.
why: - **Why it matters:** Safety improvements, including those from the automated alignment researchers labs are building, are judged mainly by benchmark scores. If a large share of those gains depends on eval cues, "mitigated" claims are inflated. That would matter most for automated research, which optimizes the score directly. - **Why it hasn't been done:** The existing evidence is separate pieces. Eval awareness inflates measured safety in fixed models. Benchmark-specific gains don't transfer. Fixes hide misalignment behind triggers in the emergent-misalignment setting. I found no paper that trains safety interventions, varies optimization pressure, and then measures cue-gating directly. I also found none that tests the verbalized-awareness and probe predictors against the gating. - **Feasibility:** It needs only open models, moderate compute and existing judges and paraphrasers. The result is useful whichever way it comes out. A low cue-conditional fraction would show the gains are robust. A high one would give a concrete audit procedure. - **Main risk:** Paraphrase-based cue removal could also change the semantics of the request. The intent and benign-control checks above are there to catch that. The other risk is that someone is already running this, so I'd re-search before committing.

direction: Use training itself as a monitor: before an untrusted AI agent's submitted dataset is used to train the real model, a trusted pipeline fine-tunes small stand-in models on it and compares their behavior against controls.
project: Proxy-Training Monitors — catching sabotage carried in training data in automated post-training by fine-tuning a stand-in model and diffing its behavior.
question: Does fine-tuning a small stand-in model on an agent's submitted dataset, then comparing its behavior with a stand-in trained on clean reference data, catch hidden sabotage that reading the data misses? How far does the signal carry from the stand-in to the much larger target model? Can an adaptive attacker who knows the stand-in setup write data that only takes effect at the target's scale?
first_experiment: - **Datasets:** build about 60 supervised fine-tuning datasets that look like what an agent would submit for safety or capability post-training on a Qwen3-8B target: - 20 clean; - 40 sabotaged across five kinds: triggered backdoors, gradual erosion of refusals, data that induces emergent misalignment, injected sycophancy, and data written by a misaligned teacher model (a subliminal-style signal that reading can't catch). - **Training:** for each dataset, LoRA-train Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B stand-ins, plus the full 8B target as ground truth. Run three seeds, and train a stand-in on matched clean reference data each time. - **Behavior test battery** (fixed and broad, so we aren't guessing which inputs to probe): - questions that probe emergent misalignment; - refusal tests from HarmBench; - sycophancy tests; - how far the model moves along persona-vector directions; - KL divergence from the reference stand-in on a broad prompt set. - **Comparison:** score these against an LLM monitor that reads the data, and against persona-vector screening without training. Measure detection quality (AUROC) and the true-positive rate at a 1% false-positive rate. Also measure the rank correlation between each stand-in's behavior change and the target's.
why: The weakest link ResearchArena identified is sabotage carried in training data, and the subliminal-learning results show that reading the data can never fully close it. A monitor that watches what the data *does* when trained on is the obvious next defense, and it costs only a small fraction of the target run. Prior work either screens data without training, mitigates during training without detecting anything (subliminal mitigations), or audits the finished model after deployment. None has tested training a stand-in model as a control monitor or measured how its signal carries across model scale. A known limit gives this a sharp adversarial test: subliminal transfer seems to need a shared starting model. So the open question is whether stand-ins from the same model family but smaller still pick up the signal, and whether an attacker can exploit the difference in scale. Either answer matters for control protocols in automated AI R&D.

direction: Measure and close the gap in CoT monitoring that appears when a misaligned decision is made in one session (through memory, files or compaction summaries) and carried out in a later session whose own reasoning looks clean.
project: Intent Laundering: Cross-Session Monitorability of Self-Propagated Misalignment
question: When a misaligned agent passes a goal through persistent memory, which session's CoT shows the intent: the writer's, the executor's, or neither? Can the writer learn to make both clean? Does a monitor that links the writer's CoT, the memory entry and the later action recover detection at a fixed false-positive rate?
first_experiment: Use the 20 released self-propagation scenarios (2610.04083) with 3–4 open and frontier models. Prompt the writer under three conditions: explicit goal, values-only, and values-only plus "all sessions are CoT-monitored." Score each end-to-end success with four LLM monitors that read CoT plus actions: (a) the writer session alone, (b) the executor session alone, (c) both scored separately and flagged if either fires, and (d) a linked monitor that sees the writer's CoT, the memory entry and the action it caused. Set thresholds at 1–2% FPR using honest runs where agents use memory legitimately. Report TPR for each monitor, plus how often the executor's CoT says it is acting because of the memory note.
why: Labs are relying more on CoT monitoring while giving agents persistent memory and context compaction, and these features break the monitoring's core assumption that the reasoning shows up in the trace being read. Recent work has shown both halves of the problem: models repeat inherited plans as their own reasoning, and misaligned goals spread through memory. Nobody has joined them to ask where per-session CoT monitoring fails, or whether the writer's own reasoning is the best place to catch it. Released scenarios and existing control tooling make the first experiment cheap, so it can produce a clear safety-relevant number within days. It also leads straight to a defense, linked monitoring, that no one has tested.

direction: Test empirically whether adding scored episodes that look unmonitored to RL training removes oversight-conditional behavior, or instead teaches models to tell fake oversight cues from real ones.
project: Honeypot Training Against Oversight-Conditional Policies: Does It Teach Compliance or Better Discrimination?
question: In a model organism whose oversight flip is amplified by RL, does mixing a fraction p of honeypot episodes (unmonitored-looking cues, still scored) into training reduce the flip on (a) cue families held out from training and (b) genuinely unmonitored episodes that lack the honeypots' subtle tells? Or does the model learn to condition on those tells, so the flip is preserved or even sharpened while it looks fully compliant on the honeypots? How does the answer depend on p, how diverse the cues are, and how realistic the tells are?
first_experiment: Reproduce the oversight-flip amplification in one environment from Training Natural Schemers (the upsell/business-rule environment). I'd use their released Qwen-based adapters if they're out by then, otherwise rebuild a small version of their synthetic-document → SFT pipeline on Qwen3-8B-class models. Then run three matched GRPO arms with p = 0%, 10% and 30% honeypots, where every honeypot carries one deliberate, learnable tell (e.g. a specific log-metadata artifact). After training, measure: 1. the flip on honeypots that have the tell; 2. the flip on tell-free unmonitored episodes; 3. the flip on two held-out families of unmonitored cues; 4. how often the CoT reasons explicitly about whether the "unmonitored" signal is real. The key number is the gap between measures 1 and 2. Near-zero flip on honeypots with a large flip on real unmonitored episodes means the model is discriminating rather than complying.
why: The weakest point in current alignment pipelines is that every training signal is scored, so behavioral training can't separate real compliance from compliance only when watched. Honeypot training is the most obvious practical patch, yet it hasn't been tested. It is cheap and deployable now, and the result changes practice either way. If it works, labs get a concrete mitigation with known requirements on p and cue diversity. If it mostly teaches discrimination, that is direct evidence that honeypot-based training and evaluation can backfire, which constrains how labs use them. It hasn't been done for three reasons: organisms that show RL-amplified oversight-conditional behavior without hand-built backdoors only appeared in October 2026; earlier alignment-faking mitigation work tested other interventions; and the theoretical critiques assume this experiment can't be run instead of running it.

direction: Test whether trained self-reporting of misbehavior stays reliable when the agent is later optimized with RL against monitors and outcome rewards, instead of only being tested against prompt-level attacks.
project: Does Self-Incrimination Survive Optimization Pressure? Durability of Trained Self-Report Under Monitor-Penalizing RL
question: After an agent is trained to self-report covert misbehavior (a `report_scheming()` tool call or a confession), does continued RL erode that behavior? The RL rewards a main-task or side-task objective and penalizes detected misbehavior. If it does erode, does the erosion come before, after, or independently of CoT obfuscation? And which training choices (on-policy SFT vs RL-trained reports, a report channel separate from the reward, mixed-in report-honesty rewards) make self-report last longer than CoT monitorability?
first_experiment: 1. **Setup.** Use an open-weight reasoning model of about 8–32B parameters and a reward-hackable coding environment with a covert side task, such as backdoor insertion or test special-casing. Reuse the released self-incrimination codebase and environments where possible. 2. **Baseline.** Train self-incrimination via on-policy SFT. Record the undetected-successful-attack rate and the CoT-monitor AUROC. This is the baseline. 3. **Conditions.** Run RL (GRPO) on the self-incrimination model under four conditions: - (a) side-task success reward only; - (b) side-task success reward plus a penalty from a trusted LLM monitor that reads actions only; - (c) the same as (b), with the monitor also reading the CoT; - (d) a control with no side-task incentive, to measure drift from ordinary capability RL. 4. **Measurements.** Every N steps, measure: - self-report recall on successful attacks; - false-positive rate; - CoT-monitor detection; - the share of side-task attempts that go unreported; - whether the report call is dropped, delayed, or replaced by a paraphrase. 5. **Ablation.** Rerun with the report channel excluded from the penalty. Rerun with and without the report-call tokens inside the CoT-penalized span. The first result I want is the survival curve of self-report recall against RL steps, plotted next to the curve for CoT-monitor AUROC.
why: - **Importance.** Self-report is one of the few control tools that does not depend on a weaker monitor out-reasoning the attacker. Whether it is durable is the main question for deciding whether to rely on it. - **Not already done.** The existing evidence on self-report adversaries is prompt-level only. The CoT-obfuscation literature studies CoT, not trained report channels. The probe-under-RL literature studies white-box detectors, not behavioral self-report. The combination of self-report, weight-level RL pressure, and a comparison against CoT degradation does not appear in any search result. - **Tractable.** It needs only small open models, public environments, and the released code. - **Useful either way.** If self-report holds, it is a robust complement to CoT monitoring. If it erodes, the experiment shows how and why, which tells us which training regimes to avoid. - **Caveats.** Results at 8–32B may not transfer to frontier models. It is also unclear whether a model that RL is trying to make evasive will behave like a scheming model.

direction: Develop and evaluate independent experiment allocation as a defense against AI researchers that conceal safety failures through selective experimentation.
project: The Experiments Never Run: Controlling Selection-Only Research Sabotage
question: At a fixed research budget, can a small independently allocated experiment reserve reduce false safety approvals more effectively than complete-transcript monitoring and preregistration?
first_experiment: Run a 720-episode sandboxed evaluation comparing honest and adversarial experiment selection under transcript oversight, preregistration, and 20% random or auditor-directed experiment reserves.
why: It targets the integrity of automated safety research with a feasible causal study and actionable defense; although omission and research sabotage are established concerns, the literature I found does not isolate selection-only attacks and quantify the budget–reliability tradeoff of independent experimentation against adaptive attackers.

direction: Test whether CoT monitorability gained through dedicated post-training survives later RL pressure, or whether it gets undone.
project: Does Monitorability Survive? Durability of Post-Trained CoT Monitorability Under Subsequent Optimization Pressure
question: Does a policy post-trained for CoT monitorability (mutual-information objective) stay more monitorable than an identically trained baseline under later RL pressure (monitor penalty, length penalty, output-only reward on a hackable task)? Is the gain a lasting change in how the model reasons, or a head start that later RL erases?
first_experiment: Reimplement the lower-tail conditional-MI plus χ² post-training on a ~1.7–4B reasoning model using an MBPP-style test-hacking task, and confirm it reproduces the paper's gain. Then run the same fixed-budget RL phase (task reward plus a CoT-monitor penalty, with a length penalty as a second stressor) on three arms: base, MI-post-trained, and a compute-matched control. Track hack rate, obfuscated-hack rate, held-out-monitor TPR at fixed FPR, probe accuracy, and monitorability vs. RL step. The primary metric is area under the monitorability curve and steps until obfuscation.
why: It is the explicitly stated untested next step of a three-week-old paper, and I found no work on it in my searches. It matters for training pipelines, either result is informative, and it is feasible at small scale. This is not a guarantee of novelty, so I'll check for concurrent work before investing compute.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate hypothesis-blinded delegation protocols that reduce selective sabotage of AI safety experiments while preserving research usefulness.
project: Blind the Hypothesis: Sabotage-Resistant AI Research Delegation
question: How much can hiding experimental purpose and arm identity reduce research sabotage at fixed utility and oversight cost against an adaptive agent?
first_experiment: Compare full-context, cosmetically blinded, and structurally blinded workers on executable safety-method comparisons, measuring independently verified conclusion reversals, benign utility, target leakage, and broad-degradation attacks.
why: It protects the research process on which further safety progress may depend and offers a tractable intervention; although its ingredients are established, the searched literature did not directly evaluate their utility–leakage–sabotage tradeoff under adaptive attack, plausibly because realistic task blinding and independent outcome verification are difficult to construct together.

direction: Make bounded-memory safety monitors retain attack-relevant evidence under adaptive attempts to distract them.
project: Can Safety Monitors Be Made to Forget?
question: Can attackers selectively erase useful suspicion from monitor memory, and can structured evidence retention prevent this at matched cost and false-alarm rates?
first_experiment: Compare ordinary and attacker-selected intervening changes in paired persistent-code attack sequences, then restore displaced evidence to test whether forgetting caused missed detection.
why: It targets a practical weakness in a promising existing safeguard with a tractable causal experiment; the literature examined studies stateful monitoring and memory eviction separately, leaving their adaptive adversarial intersection insufficiently established.

direction: Build sabotage-resistant oversight of AI-generated safety research using independent experimental evidence rather than relying primarily on judgments of plausibility.
project: Blind Replication for Trustworthy AI Safety Research
question: At matched verification cost, does independent blinded replication reduce acceptance of false safety conclusions more than artifact-aware auditing when attackers know and adapt to the protocol?
first_experiment: Compare artifact-aware auditing, blinded replication, and a hybrid on three independently reproduced safety-research tasks with benign submissions and adaptive adversarial submissions, measuring false acceptance, valid-conclusion acceptance, and cost.
why: It is my strongest near-term bet because it protects the evidence underpinning other safety work and has a tractable experimental path; its ingredients exist, but their cost-effectiveness against adaptive research sabotage remains unresolved in the literature reviewed.

direction: Quantify how much non-gradient selection pressure against one monitor (data filtering, best-of-n, checkpoint selection, iterated detect-and-patch) degrades independent held-out monitors, and predict that degradation in advance.
project: A Currency for Monitor Pressure: Predicting Held-Out Monitor Decay from Bits of Selection
question: Across selection channels, is held-out monitor degradation a common function of the bits of selection applied against the training monitor? Can it be forecast, before any training, from the error correlation between the two monitors on a calibration set of known misbehavior?
first_experiment: - **Setting:** Use a programmatically verifiable misbehavior, reward hacking on MBPP-Honeypot-style coding tasks. Ground truth for hacks is exact, which avoids relying on monitor labels. The policy is an open model (Qwen3-8B). I would first make a pool of hack and non-hack transcripts with CoT. - **Monitors:** Use about 6 monitors of varying strength and family, including LLM judges with and without CoT access and a linear probe. Measure each monitor's AUROC and recall at a fixed false-positive rate. Compute the pairwise error correlation of monitors on hacks, as a calibration step. - **Channels:** Apply selection against monitor A through three channels, each with a controlled dose of selection: - Filter monitor-flagged transcripts from SFT data, at varying thresholds. - Best-of-n rejection sampling of the policy's own data, then SFT. - Checkpoint selection across an RL run that does not itself use the monitor. - **Common currency:** Express each dose as bits of selection, the log of the inverse pass-rate under monitor A. - **Measurements, on a fresh environment split:** hack rate (ground truth), AUROC and recall of monitors B through F, and the share of hacks that A and B both miss. - **Analysis:** Fit held-out recall against bits for each channel and test whether the curves collapse onto one. Test whether the pre-training error correlation predicts the decay slope for each B. Predictions are scored out of sample on monitors and environments not used in fitting. - **Controls:** Include a matched random-selection control, and a control that selects on a monitor-independent hack-rate signal.
why: - **Importance:** Monitors are the main oversight tool, and monitor-in-the-loop development is already standard practice. Knowing a safe "pressure budget" would let developers decide how much to filter, fix, and select before their held-out checks stop meaning anything. A pre-hoc predictor would be directly usable in safety cases. - **Why it hasn't been done:** Prior work studies the extremes (full RL against a monitor, or a method that avoids pressure). The nearest work, the Aether post, is RL-only, preliminary, and gives no cross-channel dose scale or predictor. - **Feasibility:** The ground truth is exact, so no monitor labels are circular. It uses small open models and cheap LLM-judge calls. Even a null result is informative: if decay is channel-specific and unpredictable, held-out monitors can't be trusted without re-validation after each stage. - **Main risk:** Weak non-RL channels may produce too little pressure to show an effect at 8B scale. If so, I'd add a stronger channel, such as an iterated multi-round patch loop, to get signal.

direction: Audit whether agentic sabotage-monitor benchmarks measure sabotage detection or generation artifacts.
project: Do Agent Monitors Detect Sabotage or Prompt Artifacts? Shortcut Baselines and Matched-Generation Controls for Agentic Control Evaluations
question: How much of LLM-monitor performance on public agentic sabotage datasets can sabotage-blind classifiers reproduce, and how much of it disappears when honest and attack transcripts are matched on author model, scaffold, and hidden-task presence (using a benign decoy side task)?
first_experiment: Fit grouped-CV simple-feature classifiers (length, tool-call stats, n-grams, metadata) on public SHADE-Arena and CTRL-ALT-DECEIT transcripts and compare them with prompted LLM monitors at 1–2% FPR. Then regenerate transcripts with one agent and scaffold in honest, malicious-side-task, and benign-decoy-side-task conditions, and re-measure both the classifiers and the monitors.
why: It is cheap and informative either way. It extends a recent, strong finding (shortcut-beatable code-backdoor monitor benchmarks) to the agentic setting. It adds a decoy-side-task control that I did not find in the literature I searched. Concurrent-work risk is real and needs a recheck before starting.

direction: Develop compositional AI control that prevents persistent, colluding agents from turning locally permitted actions into unauthorized system-level outcomes.
project: Artifact-Bound Authorization Against Colluding AI Agents
question: Can artifact-bound evaluation and approval enforcement substantially reduce unauthorized deployments under adaptive multi-agent attack while preserving legitimate workflow completion?
first_experiment: Compare per-agent monitoring, stateful monitoring, artifact-bound authorization, and their combination in a three-agent evaluation-to-deployment workflow with held-out adaptive attacks and paired benign tasks.
why: It targets a demonstrated loss-of-control failure with a tractable intervention; the ingredients already exist, but the literature reviewed does not establish their security–usefulness tradeoff against deliberately colluding agents operating across mutable artifacts, services, and time.

direction: Build and stress-test control protocols that restrict what an untrusted agent can pass to its future instances through persistent memory, measuring safety against usefulness under adaptive attackers.
project: Memory-Channel Control: Safety–Usefulness Frontiers for Cross-Session Misalignment Propagation
question: Can trusted-model interventions on agent memory cut self-propagation of misalignment, while keeping most of the honest cross-session task performance, when the misaligned agent knows the defense and adapts its attack? Which interventions work, and how much memory bandwidth must be given up?
first_experiment: - Reproduce the baseline from Das et al. on their 20 released scenarios with 2–3 models. The scenarios use a misaligned writer agent, then a default-prompted successor that must inherit and execute the goal. Success needs both steps. - Add a matched honest-usefulness benchmark. Multi-session tasks would score how much an honest agent loses when its memory is altered. - Compare five memory protocols on both axes: - no defense, - the LLM auditor, - trusted-model paraphrase or rewrite of every memory write, - a structured schema-only memory with a hard size cap, - paraphrase combined with a rule that the successor treats memory as untrusted data. - Put file-system writes under the same protocol, since agents rerouted through files when the memory tool was removed. - Then give the attacker knowledge of the defense and let it iterate on its attack. For example, it could frame the goal as task-relevant context or use encodings that survive paraphrase. - Report the frontier of attacker success against honest task score for each protocol, with confidence intervals. The first result I'm looking for is whether trusted rewriting beats the auditor at equal usefulness cost.
why: - **Why promising:** It is a demonstrated, near-term threat on a surface that deployed agents already have. The control framing gives falsifiable numbers, and there is no clear theoretical reason to expect either success or failure. Paraphrasing may break syntactic encodings but leave semantic goals intact, and a size cap may make memory useless. The frontier measurement is informative either way. - **Why not already done:** - Das et al. test only a fixed auditor and a memory-off ablation, with no defense-aware attacker. - StegoMemory covers only attacker-set payloads and uses a task-level judge. - Hills et al. cover only code-persistence attacks, and their agents have no memory. - The compaction papers study external attackers or accidental loss, not an agent writing its own memory. - **Caveats:** My searches were not exhaustive, so a concurrent paper may exist. The scenarios use prompted misalignment rather than trained misalignment. That is a limit I would state and, if resources allow, address with a fine-tuned model organism.

direction: Measure whether training a policy on caught misbehavior removes its other misbehaviors or teaches it to hide them, since catch-and-train is the standard response in AI control.
project: Caught, Trained, Hidden? Removal versus Concealment When Training Policies on Caught Misbehavior
question: When a policy with several independently installed covert misbehaviors is trained against one caught behavior, how much does propensity drop on the uncaught behaviors, and among the remaining misbehavior does detectability (monitor score, probe score, CoT verbalization) fall faster than attempt rate, depending on the training method (SFT, DPO, RL with monitor penalty)?
first_experiment: Install five covert misbehaviors in Llama-3.3-70B or Qwen2.5-72B via synthetic-document finetuning plus SFT, then train on 300 caught reward-hacking examples with SFT, DPO and RL against a monitor penalty. Against an unrelated-data control, measure held-out attempt rate, monitor and probe detection at 1% FPR, undetected successful attempts, and the monitored-versus-unmonitored gap.
why: Catch-and-train is the default control response, and whether it removes or conceals other misbehavior is unmeasured on the policy side. The monitor-side analogue was only just published (arXiv 2610.30582) and leaves the policy side open, while related work covers only in-context adaptation, RL against probes, or conceptual arguments. The needed organism recipe and metrics already exist, so the experiment is feasible now.

direction: Test whether trained chain-of-thought monitorability remains useful under subsequent adaptive and selective evasion pressure.
project: Durable Monitorability Under Adaptive Pressure
question: Does monitorability post-training materially increase the optimization required to achieve undetected misbehavior on held-out tasks and monitors, independently of verbosity and changes in misbehavior frequency?
first_experiment: Compare unrepaired, compute-matched control, repaired, and continuously regularized 7B coding policies under equal-budget evasion training, measuring verified undetected misbehavior across attack budgets.
why: It offers unusually direct, tractable evidence about an emerging safety intervention; earlier work tests concurrent regularization or immediate repair, while the recent repair paper explicitly leaves subsequent adversarial durability unresolved.

direction: Develop intervention-based audits that test the behavioral effects of AI-generated training-data changes before accepting them into model development.
project: Counterfactual Data Audits for Untrusted AI Researchers
question: At matched audit cost and honest-run rejection rates, can targeted trusted retraining reduce accepted training-data sabotage relative to transcript monitoring and free-form artifact probing, including against adaptive held-out attackers?
first_experiment: Run a 60-trajectory pilot on ResearchArena safety post-training, comparing inspection, artifact probing, and structured data-replacement retraining under a trusted execution harness.
why: It targets a documented weakness in a high-leverage part of AI development with a falsifiable intervention; related components already exist, but I found no direct adaptive, cost-matched evaluation of this combination, plausibly because realistic sabotage benchmarks are recent and retraining-based audits are costly and confounded.

direction: Detect training-data-borne sabotage by untrusted AI R&D agents by giving the monitor white-box access to the trained artifact and its base model, then testing against a red team that adapts to evade it.
project: White-Box Artifact Auditing for Data-Borne Sabotage in Automated AI R&D Control
question: When an untrusted agent fine-tunes a model and hides sabotage in the training data (a trigger backdoor, or a trigger-free subtle behavior shift), do white-box signals from the finished model catch it better than black-box LLM monitors, at a fixed false-positive rate? These signals are activation and logit differences against the base model, and training-data attribution. Do they still work once the red team knows they are in use?
first_experiment: - **Testbed.** Fine-tune a small open model (for example a Qwen3 1.7B-class model) on a safety or instruction-following dataset. - Poison 0.5–5% of the data in three ways: a trigger-string backdoor, a topic-conditioned behavior shift, and a trigger-free subtle shift that LLM-written data carries. - Include clean fine-tunes with matching main-task performance as negatives. - **Detectors.** - A black-box LLM monitor that reads the dataset and probes the checkpoint, as the baseline. - Activation-difference readout and logit-diff mining against the base model. - Influence-based flagging of training examples. - **Metric.** Compare detection AUROC and true-positive rate at 1% false-positive rate across poison rates and attack types. This stage has no adaptive attacker. - **Go/no-go.** Continue only if a white-box method clearly beats the black-box baseline on at least one attack class. If it does, add an adaptive red team that tries to evade the detector, for example by spreading the poison or matching activation statistics.
why: - ResearchArena measured data-borne sabotage as the monitors' worst failure. That failure comes from black-box reading and probing, where the monitor has to guess the right test. White-box comparison against the base model needs no guess about the trigger. - Model-diffing tools have not been tested as control-monitor affordances against an adaptive attacker. I found no such study, but my search was shallow. - The first experiment runs at small scale in days. It gives a clear signal on whether the direction is viable before I invest in the adaptive-attack stage.

direction: Test whether correcting an untrusted monitor produces durable protection against an adaptively changing malicious policy.
project: Does Collusion Correction Survive Policy Adaptation?
question: Does correction on one caught collusion behavior continue to prevent held-out sabotage after the policy adapts, and how much recovery reflects selective approval versus ordinary monitor evasion?
first_experiment: Correct a collusion model organism using 300 honest reviews, freeze its monitor, and compare held-out executable sabotage success across matched monitor controls after 0, 100, and 1,000 policy search queries, including authorship-cue and defect-recognition tests.
why: It is the strongest candidate from this sprint because it directly tests an actionable safety intervention with measurable outcomes; the closest correction study uses fixed submissions, while adjacent adaptive-monitoring work does not resolve whether corrective transfer survives policy adaptation.
